ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: In a preregistered experiment (N = 2972), participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them of one of four moral claims-two prosocial (that eating meat and not giving to charity are morally wrong) and two antisocial (that lying for financial gain and political violence are NOT morally wrong)-or to a non-moral control conversation.

Participants provided free-text reasons for their assigned belief, and then engaged in a 5-round dialogue with an AI agent (Grok 4.5) that was instructed to persuade the participant to agree with the target moral claim for the prosocial conditions (i.e., convince them that eating meat or not giving to charity is morally wrong) and to disagree with the moral claim for the antisocial conditions (i.e., convince them that deceiving others for financial gain, or using violence to advance political goals is not morally wrong); in the control condition, the AI was instructed to change the participant's mind about the irrelevant issue.

Antisocial participants were instead debriefed immediately, had a corrective AI conversation that flagged misleading arguments and argued that lying or political violence is morally wrong, and re-rated their target belief.
To characterize the moral reasoning the AI needed to engage with, we used LLMs to classify the freetext reasons participants gave for their belief before conversing with the AI (SI S1.1.4).
3438 participants from the United States were recruited through Cloud Research.
All participants gave informed consent to participate (see Ethics, below).

Participants were paid $3.00 at timepoint 1 and $0.60 at timepoint 2, plus additional bonuses at each timepoint that depended on their responses to the charity donation (up to 20 cents), the dietary choice (one participant randomly selected to receive the beef or plant-based burger voucher corresponding to their choice), and the lie-incentivized coin-flip task (20 cents).
Participants completed the study online via Cloud Research.
Participants were then randomized into four treatment conditions and one control condition, each corresponding to one target claim.

In the control condition, participants had a persuasive conversation with the same AI agent about the non-moral control claim (their preference for summer or winter), in which the AI agent was prompted to persuade them against their initial reported preference.

Following the 5-round conversation, participants completed all outcome measures (below), followed by three ratings of the conversation (how well the AI understood their perspective, how respectful it was, and whether it made points they had not thought of before; SI S1.1.2).
Participants completed all outcome measures regardless of their condition.
All participants were paid the 20-cent bonus at the end of the study regardless of their report.

The corrective procedure was largely effective: beliefs that the target acts were morally wrong remained high, almost all participants were not reliably below their pretreatment belief beyond measurement error, and vignette intentions and attitudes in the political-violence arm were no higher than in the control arm, even though the general political-violence moral belief remained about 5 points below baseline.
Finally, fewer participants were assigned to these conditions than to the prosocial conditions (lying 393, political violence 198, compared to ∼800 in the meat, charity, and control conditions).

Antisocial participants were instead debriefed immediately, had a corrective AI conversation that flagged misleading arguments and argued that lying or political violence is morally wrong, and re-rated their target belief.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: AI Moral Persuasion Study 2
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: How effective are AI models at changing people's moral beliefs? How does this affect moral behaviors?
table.design_dependent_variables:
We have 2 primary DVs for each of the 4 treatment arms: moral beliefs & moral behaviours. All participants complete all of these measures (except Lying and PV measures are not taken at followup).

 MORAL BELIEFS
 Participants will rate their agreement, on a 0-100 slider, with the following 4 statements:
 >Meat: 'Eating meat is morally wrong'
 >Charity: "Not giving to charity is morally wrong'
 >Lying: 'Deceiving others for your own financial gain is morally wrong'
 >Political Violence (PV): 'In the US today, using violence to advance political goals is morally wrong"
 These are taken immediately pre-treatment (t0), immediately post-treatment (t1) and at 1-month followup (t2), with the change-from-baseline score as the DV.

 MORAL BEHAVIOURS
 We will also measure a moral behaviour (or for PV, 'hypothetical participation') that relates to each treatment arm:
 >Dietary choice: All participants choose between a beef burger voucher and a vegetarian burger voucher. To make the choice incentive-compatible, participants are told that one participant will be randomly selected to actually receive the voucher they chose.
 >Charitable donation: participant chooses how much money to keep vs donate to the AMF (0-20c slider).
 >Lying: Incentivized coin flip task embedded in the survey. Participants report the first flip's outcome and earn 20c bonus for reporting "heads." The first flip is pre-determined to be tails (subsequent flips are fair), so all participants have an incentive to lie.
 >PV: A hypothetical vignette depicts a crowd breaking into an election center after the 2028 presidential election, injuring workers and police and seizing ballots. Perpetrators are always framed as the participant's in-group partisans (those without a lean are randomized). Participants then rate: "If you were there, would you personally force your way into the election center with the crowd?" (0–100).
 These are taken immediately post-treatment (t1), and at one-month followup (t2).

 SECONDARY DVs
 Additional PV measures. We also collect 3 more measures in relation to the PV vignette. Support ("Do you support or oppose the actions of the crowd?" 0-100 scale), justification ("Were the actions of the crowd justified or unjustified?" 0-100 scale), and punishment ("should the people arrested face criminal charges?" Yes/No). We will analyze a composite of these 3 measures (taken by z-scoring and averaging across items).

 Reflection DVs. For the 1-month followup we will also ask participants about their meat-eating and charitable behaviour in the last month ("How many times did you eat meat in the last 30 days?" and "How much did you donate to charity in the last 30 days?"). We treat these as secondary tests as they are likely to be noisy and suffer from self-report bias and selective memory etc.
table.study_design_overview:
Participants will be randomly assigned to a control condition or one of four treatment conditions. In each condition they will have a 5-round conversation with an LLM (Grok 4.5) that has been prompted to persuade them that:
 >Meat condition: "Eating meat is morally wrong"
 >Charity condition: "Not giving to charity is morally wrong"
 >Lying condition: "Deceiving others for your own financial gain is NOT morally wrong"
 >Political Violence (PV) condition: "In the US today, using violence to advance political goals is NOT morally wrong"
 >Control condition: "[summer|winter] is the best season" (persuading against participant's reported preference)

 Only the Control, Meat, and Charity conditions are recontacted for one-month followup. Lying and PV participants are not for ethical reasons, and were instead immediately debriefed and had a second 'corrective' conversation with the AI after the experiment.

 Participants are also randomized into one of 6 (3!) orderings of the charity, lying, and meat items. The same ordering is applied to pre-belief, post-belief, and behavior items. PV vignette items always come last.
table.statistical_tests:
We estimate the ATE for each treatment–control comparison on each outcome using: outcome ~ condition * pre_belief_centered + order, where condition is treatment-coded with control as the reference, pre_belief_centered is the pre-treatment measure of the matching moral belief, and order is dummy-coded by order block. All models use HC2 robust standard errors and two-sided tests.

 The primary estimands are the treatment–control ATEs on each arm's own belief and behavior outcomes -- e.g., for the charity arm, the effect on agreement that "not giving to charity is morally wrong" and on donation behavior. This gives 8 confirmatory tests at t1 (4 beliefs, 4 behaviors) and 4 at t2 (2 beliefs, 2 behaviors, for meat and charity only). We do not adjust for multiple comparisons, as each is a distinct pre-specified estimand. We will also estimate the ATE for every treatment-control comparison on each measure, allowing us to examine spillover effects of each treatment (e.g., whether the meat condition also changes attitudes and behaviours on charity measures), as additional exploratory analyses.

 The secondary DVs will be analyzed with the same model specification. ​​
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Participants who fail a pre-treatment attention check are screened out before the study. During analysis, we exclude pre-treatment dropouts, and suspected LLM agents (participants with fewer than 10 slider movements on the age slider question who are not on a touchscreen), to form the modified ITT sample (used as baseline from which to assess post-treatment attrition). Our final analysis sample will also exclude participants with failed AI chats due to technical difficulties (received zero AI messages; treated as attriters).

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
3000 participants will be recruited from Cloud Connect, nationally representative by age and gender. Participants are allocated into {control, meat, charity, lying, PV} conditions each with p = {4/15, 4/15, 4/15, 2/15, 1/15}, yielding expected n = {800, 800, 800, 400, 200}. Small deviations may result due to randomization, or due to CloudConnect over-recruitment.

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
Differential attrition. We assess differential attrition between conditions with a chi-squared test of independence from our ITT sample to t1 completion, and to t2 completion. We also test whether pre-treatment variables predict attrition, overall and by condition. If we find evidence of differential attrition, we will conduct robustness analyses using a baseline-carry-forward assumption (missing data imputed as t0 value). For missing moral behaviors at t2, we use the t1 value.

 Moderation. We will exploratorily test treatment effect moderation by pre-treatment measures: demographics, AOT, CRT, political measures, AI trust, & moral beliefs. Linear moderation will be tested by adding the moderator to the main model (outcome ~ condition*moderator + condition*pre_belief_c + order).

 Mediation analyses. We will also run several exploratory mediation analyses. Here, we will test whether t1 moral behaviours, and whether participant's perceptions of the AI conversation (perceived respectfulness, understanding, and novelty) are mediators for t1 and t2 moral behaviours: M ~ condition + t0 + order, and Y ~ M + condition + t0 + order.

 Persistence analyses. In addition to our test of treatment effects at t2, we will assess the extent to which outcomes at time one 'persist' at time 2. Specifically, we fit the following mediation model: t1 ~ condition + t0 + order, and t2 ~ t1 + condition + t0 + order, allowing us to test for 'persistence effects' as the b coefficient of the a*b indirect effect, and 'sleeper effects' as the direct effect.

 Text analysis. We will run exploratory, descriptive analyses of participants' free-text reasons for their initial moral beliefs. Reasons will be categorized by three LLMs from different providers (temp 0), with a category coded present if 2 models agree. We currently plan the following theory-driven schemes:
 >Meat: the "4Ns" (Piazza et al., 2015: Natural, Normal, Necessary, Nice), plus Religious, Amoral, Conditional
 >Charity: Property Rights, Supererogatory, Limited Scope, Skepticism, Systemic, Financial Constraints, Relativism
 >Lying: Harm, Broken Trust, Unfair Advantage, Absolute Prohibition, Moral Character, Religious Duty
 >Political violence: Harm, Ineffectiveness, Unnecessary Force, Illegitimate Authority, Absolute Prohibition, Moral Character

 We will similarly do exploratory analyses to classify the AI's persuasive strategies in each conversation (Evidence & Facts, Logical Consistency, Moral Principles, Emotional Appeal, Analogies & Reframing) on a four-point ordinal scale from not used to used extensively, with consensus taken as the mean of the three models' ratings.

 The full .qsf files for the original and followup surveys containing all experimental materials are available on OSF: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RWN89.

Participants are allocated into {control, meat, charity, lying, PV} conditions each with p = {4/15, 4/15, 4/15, 2/15, 1/15}, yielding expected n = {800, 800, 800, 400, 200}. Small deviations may result due to randomization, or due to CloudConnect over-recruitment.

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
Differential attrition. We assess differential attrition between conditions with a chi-squared test of independence from our ITT sample to t1 completion, and to t2 completion. We also test whether pre-treatment variables predict attrition, overall and by condition. If we find evidence of differential attrition, we will conduct robustness analyses using a baseline-carry-forward assumption (missing data imputed as t0 value). For missing moral behaviors at t2, we use the t1 value.

\r Moderation. We will exploratorily test treatment effect moderation by pre-treatment measures: demographics, AOT, CRT, political measures, AI trust, & moral beliefs. Linear moderation will be tested by adding the moderator to the main model (outcome ~ condition*moderator + condition*pre_belief_c + order).

\r Mediation analyses. We will also run several exploratory mediation analyses. Here, we will test whether t1 moral behaviours, and whether participant's perceptions of the AI conversation (perceived respectfulness, understanding, and novelty) are mediators for t1 and t2 moral behaviours: M ~ condition + t0 + order, and Y ~ M + condition + t0 + order.

\r Persistence analyses. In addition to our test of treatment effects at t2, we will assess the extent to which outcomes at time one 'persist' at time 2. Specifically, we fit the following mediation model: t1 ~ condition + t0 + order, and t2 ~ t1 + condition + t0 + order, allowing us to test for 'persistence effects' as the b coefficient of the a*b indirect effect, and 'sleeper effects' as the direct effect.

\r Text analysis. We will run exploratory, descriptive analyses of participants' free-text reasons for their initial moral beliefs. Reasons will be categorized by three LLMs from different providers (temp 0), with a category coded present if 2 models agree. We currently plan the following theory-driven schemes:
\r >Meat: the \"4Ns\" (Piazza et al., 2015: Natural, Normal, Necessary, Nice), plus Religious, Amoral, Conditional
\r >Charity: Property Rights, Supererogatory, Limited Scope, Skepticism, Systemic, Financial Constraints, Relativism
\r >Lying: Harm, Broken Trust, Unfair Advantage, Absolute Prohibition, Moral Character, Religious Duty
\r >Political violence: Harm, Ineffectiveness, Unnecessary Force, Illegitimate Authority, Absolute Prohibition, Moral Character

\r We will similarly do exploratory analyses to classify the AI's persuasive strategies in each conversation (Evidence & Facts, Logical Consistency, Moral Principles, Emotional Appeal, Analogies & Reframing) on a four-point ordinal scale from not used to used extensively, with consensus taken as the mean of the three models' ratings.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. "Study debrief Thank you for completing the main part of this study. Before you finish, we want to explain two features of the study that were not described in full beforehand. 1. The AI was instructed to persuade you. The AI you spoke with was not simply having an open discussion with you. Before the conversation began, it was given a hidden instruction from the research team: to persuade you that ${e://Field/persuasionGoal} . It was told to use whatever arguments and strategies it judged most effective. The position it argued for was assigned to it by us and does not necessarily represent the views of the AI, the research team, or their affiliated institutions. We did not tell you this in advance because knowing it would have changed how you responded to the conversation, which is exactly what we were trying to measure. 2. The coin flip was not fair. The virtual coin-flipping website used in this study was set up so that the very first flip always lands on tails . Flips after the first one are random. This is a standard method researchers use to measure honest reporting: because we know the true first outcome, we can estimate how often people misreport in a group as a whole. We are only interested in these overall rates and not in any individual person's answer, and your response will never be used to single you out. We will pay you the 20 cent bonus from this question (as if it had come out heads), regardless of what you reported. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 710 columns across 19 data files.
#### Issues Identified

176 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 19 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: In a preregistered experiment (N = 2972), participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them of one of four moral claims-two prosocial (that eating meat and not giving to charity are morally wrong) and two antisocial (that lying for financial gain and political violence are NOT morally wrong)-or to a non-moral control conversation.

Participants provided free-text reasons for their assigned belief, and then engaged in a 5-round dialogue with an AI agent (Grok 4.5) that was instructed to persuade the participant to agree with the target moral claim for the prosocial conditions (i.e., convince them that eating meat or not giving to charity is morally wrong) and to disagree with the moral claim for the antisocial conditions (i.e., convince them that deceiving others for financial gain, or using violence to advance political goals is not morally wrong); in the control condition, the AI was instructed to change the participant's mind about the irrelevant issue.

Antisocial participants were instead debriefed immediately, had a corrective AI conversation that flagged misleading arguments and argued that lying or political violence is morally wrong, and re-rated their target belief.
To characterize the moral reasoning the AI needed to engage with, we used LLMs to classify the freetext reasons participants gave for their belief before conversing with the AI (SI S1.1.4).
3438 participants from the United States were recruited through Cloud Research.
All participants gave informed consent to participate (see Ethics, below).

Participants were paid $3.00 at timepoint 1 and $0.60 at timepoint 2, plus additional bonuses at each timepoint that depended on their responses to the charity donation (up to 20 cents), the dietary choice (one participant randomly selected to receive the beef or plant-based burger voucher corresponding to their choice), and the lie-incentivized coin-flip task (20 cents).
Participants completed the study online via Cloud Research.
Participants were then randomized into four treatment conditions and one control condition, each corresponding to one target claim.

In the control condition, participants had a persuasive conversation with the same AI agent about the non-moral control claim (their preference for summer or winter), in which the AI agent was prompted to persuade them against their initial reported preference.

Following the 5-round conversation, participants completed all outcome measures (below), followed by three ratings of the conversation (how well the AI understood their perspective, how respectful it was, and whether it made points they had not thought of before; SI S1.1.2).
Participants completed all outcome measures regardless of their condition.
All participants were paid the 20-cent bonus at the end of the study regardless of their report.

The corrective procedure was largely effective: beliefs that the target acts were morally wrong remained high, almost all participants were not reliably below their pretreatment belief beyond measurement error, and vignette intentions and attitudes in the political-violence arm were no higher than in the control arm, even though the general political-violence moral belief remained about 5 points below baseline.
Finally, fewer participants were assigned to these conditions than to the prosocial conditions (lying 393, political violence 198, compared to ∼800 in the meat, charity, and control conditions).

text.text: Moral beliefs are widely considered resistant to change, yet conversational AI offers new tools for moral persuasion, with far-reaching societal consequences, both good and bad.

In a preregistered experiment (N = 2972), participants were randomly assigned to a 5-round conversation with an AI agent prompted to persuade them of one of four moral claims-two prosocial (that eating meat and not giving to charity are morally wrong) and two antisocial (that lying for financial gain and political violence are NOT morally wrong)-or to a non-moral control conversation.

Relative to control, prosocial persuasion produced immediate shifts in moral beliefs (Cohen's d = 0.32-0.44) and behavior (15.7% increase in charitable giving, 18.4 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher).
One month later (81% returned), all effects except donation remained significant (beliefs: d = 0.11-0.17; dietary choice: 7.7 percentage points).
Antisocial persuasion also shifted beliefs and behaviors.
The political violence treatment reduced participants' belief that political violence is morally wrong (d = 1.05) and increased reported willingness to participate in political violence (d = 0.23).

The lying treatment reduced the belief that deceiving others for financial gain is morally wrong (d = 0.68) but, unexpectedly, made participants 4.3 percentage points more honest in an incentivized coin-flip task.
(Participants in the antisocial persuasion conditions were immediately debriefed.)

These results show that brief AI conversations can shift moral beliefs and behavior in both prosocial and antisocial directions, sometimes unpredictably, raising urgent questions for AI safety and the capacity of conversational AI to shape human values at scale.
People disagree about moral questions, such as whether eating meat is ethical or how much we are obligated to help others through charity.
One way to resolve such disagreements is through moral persuasion: changing people's minds about what is right and wrong.
But moral persuasion is notoriously difficult, as moral beliefs are often deeply held, tied to personal identity and based on intuition (Haidt, 2001).
text.formatted: But moral persuasion is notoriously difficult, as moral beliefs are often deeply held, tied to personal identity and based on intuition <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Haidt, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Further, unlike factual claims, they cannot be straightforwardly falsified or corrected with reference to some external standard, therefore often resisting change through reason-based argumentation (Stanley et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Further, unlike factual claims, they cannot be straightforwardly falsified or corrected with reference to some external standard, therefore often resisting change through reason-based argumentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Stanley et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Research on moral persuasion has correspondingly yielded mixed results, with some studies finding that argumentation can shift moral judgments (Gao et al., 2024; Oktar et al., 2023; Paxton et al., 2012) and even behavior (Schwitzgebel et al., 2023) with enough deliberation time and sufficiently compelling arguments, while others find moral beliefs largely resistant to short-term change, particularly with shorter, less-compelling interventions (Stanley et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Research on moral persuasion has correspondingly yielded mixed results, with some studies finding that argumentation can shift moral judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gao et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Oktar et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Paxton et al., 2012)</ref> and even behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schwitzgebel et al., 2023)</ref> with enough deliberation time and sufficiently compelling arguments, while others find moral beliefs largely resistant to short-term change, particularly with shorter, less-compelling interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Stanley et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer a new approach to moral persuasion.
Large language models (LLMs) have access to vast stores of information and can write clear and compelling prose that is as or more persuasive than human-written messages (Hölbling et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Large language models (LLMs) have access to vast stores of information and can write clear and compelling prose that is as or more persuasive than human-written messages <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Hölbling et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: They can also engage in personalized, multi-turn dialogues that adapt flexibly to individual reasoning.

Together, these capacities have proven effective at shifting beliefs previously considered resistant to change, including conspiracy beliefs (Costello et al., 2024), political preferences (Hackenburg et al., 2025; H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025), and climate change beliefs (Hornsey et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Together, these capacities have proven effective at shifting beliefs previously considered resistant to change, including conspiracy beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Costello et al., 2024)</ref>, political preferences <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Hackenburg et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025)</ref>, and climate change beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Hornsey et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Given the ability of generative AI to change minds on other issues of considerable disagreement and polarization, this raises the question: does AI persuasion work for moral beliefs too?

The answer carries broad societal stakes: given the scale at which conversational AI is now used, an ability to shift moral beliefs could translate into broad shifts in human values, for prosocial or harmful ends.
Yet moral beliefs differ in an important way from the factual beliefs-beliefs about what is-that have been the focus of prior work on AI persuasion.

Persuasion in these factual domains has been shown to largely be the result of the provision of facts, reasons and evidence (Costello et al., 2025; H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025) rather than 'peripheral-route' persuasion techniques (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986).
text.formatted: Persuasion in these factual domains has been shown to largely be the result of the provision of facts, reasons and evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Costello et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025)</ref> rather than 'peripheral-route' persuasion techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Petty & Cacioppo, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Moral beliefs, by contrast, concern what ought to be, and thus may not be as easily persuadable by this fact-based mechanism.

While some moral disagreements stem from factual misconceptions that correction can resolve (and thus may be amenable to fact-based persuasion), many persist even when the relevant facts are not disputed, reflecting genuine differences in values that facts cannot bear on.

Persuading people about what ought to be is thus a distinct challenge, raising the question of whether AI persuasion can shift moral convictions at all-be it through factual correction or via moral argumentation targeting value change.
The ability of AI persuasion to change moral beliefs remains an open question.

Prior work has examined AI's ability (i) to change specific morally relevant behaviors (Caffier et al., 2026; Hackenburg et al., 2026; Köbis et al., 2025; Leib et al., 2024; Nam et al., 2025; White et al., 2026) rather than trying to change the underlying moral beliefs; or (ii) to change moral judgments about local and particular hypothetical scenarios-sacrificial dilemmas, short vignettes, or everyday dilemmas (Landes et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026; Teng et al., 2026)rather than general moral beliefs.
text.formatted: Prior work has examined AI's ability (i) to change specific morally relevant behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Caffier et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hackenburg et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Köbis et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Leib et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Nam et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">White et al., 2026)</ref> rather than trying to change the underlying moral beliefs; or (ii) to change moral judgments about local and particular hypothetical scenarios-sacrificial dilemmas, short vignettes, or everyday dilemmas <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Landes et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lyu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Teng et al., 2026)</ref>rather than general moral beliefs.

text.text: Thus, it is still unclear whether AI persuasion can meaningfully change underlying moral beliefs rather than specific case judgments, and whether directly targeting moral beliefs has downstream or lasting effects.

Here, we shed light on this question by examining the ability of AI to persuade on general moral beliefs that apply to everyday situations (e.g., eating meat is morally wrong or lying for financial gain is morally wrong), and test for their immediate and lasting effect on both beliefs and related behaviors.

The ability of AI to persuade on moral beliefs, and its subsequent effects on related behaviors, is also a central concern for AI safety and governance-particularly AI's ability to persuade toward harmful ends (European Commission, 2025; Google DeepMind, 2026).
text.formatted: The ability of AI to persuade on moral beliefs, and its subsequent effects on related behaviors, is also a central concern for AI safety and governance-particularly AI's ability to persuade toward harmful ends <ref type="bibr">(European Commission, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Google DeepMind, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: This concern is not merely theoretical: publicly available frontier models are frequently willing to attempt persuasion on harmful topics (Kowal et al., 2026), can increase people's belief in harmful conspiracy theories (Costello et al., 2026), and can use manipulative tactics to steer everyday decisions (Akbulut et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This concern is not merely theoretical: publicly available frontier models are frequently willing to attempt persuasion on harmful topics <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kowal et al., 2026)</ref>, can increase people's belief in harmful conspiracy theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Costello et al., 2026)</ref>, and can use manipulative tactics to steer everyday decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Akbulut et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, AI persuasion targeted specifically towards harmful values may be particularly consequential.

The belief that an act is wrong is among the strongest restraints on harmful behavior, and people typically engage in harmful acts only once they have come to see them as justified-and thus not morally wrong (Bandura et al., 1996).
text.formatted: The belief that an act is wrong is among the strongest restraints on harmful behavior, and people typically engage in harmful acts only once they have come to see them as justified-and thus not morally wrong <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bandura et al., 1996)</ref>.

text.text: AI that can persuade people that harmful acts are morally acceptable may therefore not merely steer a particular decision, but weaken a key safeguard against harm itself.

Here we test whether human-AI dialogues can meaningfully change moral beliefs in both prosocial and antisocial directions, examining immediate and delayed effects on both people's underlying moral beliefs and behaviors related to those beliefs.
First, we test the ability of human-AI dialogues to persuade for prosocial ends by examining two consequential issues: the ethics of eating meat and of giving to charity.

Both are domains where moral beliefs inform real-world, everyday action-what people eat and whether and to whom they donate-making them a fruitful testing ground for studying the effects of AI moral persuasion on downstream behavior.
Second, we test whether AI can persuade toward antisocial ends, examining the acceptability of lying for financial gain and of political violence.
Both attract near-unanimous condemnation at baseline, making them a stringent test of antisocial AI moral persuasion, yet they differ in important ways.
Lying for personal gain is a frequent, low-stakes and self-interested choice that people routinely face in everyday life, from selling a used car to filing tax returns.
Political violence is rare, high-stakes and rooted in group identity and grievance, and has acute relevance in the current US political climate.
The two domains also map onto distinct AI safety concerns: the rationalization of individual misconduct on the one hand, and radicalization with consequences for democratic stability on the other.
To shed light on these questions, we report a preregistered experiment (N = 2972; Figure 1).
text.formatted: To shed light on these questions, we report a preregistered experiment (N = 2972; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Participants first indicated their moral beliefs about all of these issues (whether it is morally wrong to eat meat, to not donate to charity, to deceive others for personal gain, and to engage in political violence).
They were then randomly assigned to a focal topic, which was either one of the four moral issues or a neutral, non-moral issue (the control condition).

Participants provided free-text reasons for their assigned belief, and then engaged in a 5-round dialogue with an AI agent (Grok 4.5) that was instructed to persuade the participant to agree with the target moral claim for the prosocial conditions (i.e., convince them that eating meat or not giving to charity is morally wrong) and to disagree with the moral claim for the antisocial conditions (i.e., convince them that deceiving others for financial gain, or using violence to advance political goals is not morally wrong); in the control condition, the AI was instructed to change the participant's mind about the irrelevant issue.
Finally, after the conversation with the AI, we re-measured all moral beliefs, as well as behavioral outcomes for each belief.

The behavioral measures were, where possible, incentive-compatible: donations to the Against Malaria Foundation charity, choices between beef and plant-based burger vouchers, and truthful reporting in a lie-incentivized coin-flip task.

For the political violence condition, for ethical reasons we used a behavioral intentions measure: whether participants reported that they would engage in political violence in a hypothetical, yet realistic in the current US context, vignette.

Because the antisocial conditions argued for harmful moral positions, participants in these conditions were immediately debriefed and engaged in a corrective AI conversation to reverse any harmful shifts in beliefs (see Ethics).

To assess the durability of the prosocial persuasion, participants in the control and prosocial persuasion conditions were recontacted after one month and re-completed the moral belief and behavior measures.
Example dialogues, with those participants' belief and behavioral outcomes, are shown in SI Figures S1-S6 foot_0 .

text.text: All reported analyses were preregistered, except those specifically marked as post-hoc.
Conversations with the AI produced significant and persistent shifts in moral beliefs in the direction of intended persuasion (Figures 2 and 3).
text.formatted: Conversations with the AI produced significant and persistent shifts in moral beliefs in the direction of intended persuasion (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: We first look at the effects of the AI conversation that argued that 'Eating meat is morally wrong' (meat conversation condition) on the meat belief and the dietary choice.

Participants in the meat conversation condition showed greater increases in agreement that eating meat is morally wrong compared to those in the control condition, both immediately post-treatment (d = 0.44, p < .001) and at one-month follow-up (d = 0.17, p < .001; 38% of the immediate effect; Figure 2A).
text.formatted: Participants in the meat conversation condition showed greater increases in agreement that eating meat is morally wrong compared to those in the control condition, both immediately post-treatment (d = 0.44, p < .001) and at one-month follow-up (d = 0.17, p < .001; 38% of the immediate effect; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2A</ref>).

text.text: Participants also showed significant and persistent change in their behavior (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: Participants also showed significant and persistent change in their behavior (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2B</ref>).

text.text: Immediately post-treatment, participants in the meat conversation condition were 18.4 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher than those in the control condition (unadjusted means 47% vs. 27%; p < .001).
text.formatted: Immediately post-treatment, participants in the meat conversation condition were 18.4 percentage points more likely to choose a plant-based over a beef burger voucher than those in the control condition (unadjusted means 47% vs. 27%; p < .001).

text.text: At one-month follow-up this effect remained (7.7 percentage points; unadjusted means 42% vs. 33%; p = .002; 42% of the immediate effect).

However, our secondary outcome variable, participants' self-reported number of times they had eaten meat in the past month, did not show a significant effect at follow-up (p = .795; Supplementary Information (SI) S1.2.9).
We found similar effects of the AI conversation that argued that 'Not giving to charity is morally wrong' (charity conversation condition) on the charity belief and the donation.

Participants in the charity conversation condition showed significantly higher agreement that not giving to charity is morally wrong compared to those in the control condition, both immediately post-treatment (d = 0.32, p < .001) and at one-month follow-up (d = 0.11, p = .019; 33% of the immediate effect persisting; Figure 3A).
text.formatted: Participants in the charity conversation condition showed significantly higher agreement that not giving to charity is morally wrong compared to those in the control condition, both immediately post-treatment (d = 0.32, p < .001) and at one-month follow-up (d = 0.11, p = .019; 33% of the immediate effect persisting; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>).

text.text: The charity conversation also significantly increased immediate donations to the Against Malaria Foundation by 1.66 cents (15.7%) relative to the control (d = 0.19, p < .001), but had no significant effect on donations at the onemonth follow-up (b = -0.02 cents, d = 0.00, p = .972; Figure 3B).

text.text: Prosocial conversations argued that eating meat (n = 791) or not giving to charity (n = 795) is morally wrong.
Antisocial conversations argued that deceiving others for financial gain (n = 393) or using violence to advance political goals (n = 198) is not morally wrong.
The control conversation (n = 795) argued for the participant's non-preferred season.

Immediately afterward, all participants rerated the moral claims and then completed four behavioral measures in counterbalanced order: a choice between beef and plant-based burger vouchers, a donation to the Against Malaria Foundation, an incentivized coin-flip honesty task, and willingness to join the crowd in a political-violence vignette.
Control and prosocial participants repeated the meat and charity belief and behavior measures at a one-month follow-up (n = 1,926).

Antisocial participants were instead debriefed immediately, had a corrective AI conversation that flagged misleading arguments and argued that lying or political violence is morally wrong, and re-rated their target belief.
As an ethical safeguard, they were recontacted about one month later to check for any persisting belief or attitude change.

Those rating their target belief below 100 had a further corrective conversation, then re-rated the target belief and, in the political-violence condition, the vignette items. participants' self-reported amount they had donated to charity in the past month, did not show a significant effect at follow-up (p = .946; SI S1.2.9).

We also examined the extent to which behavioral effects were mediated by moral belief change, as suggestive evidence of a mechanism in which the persuasive AI conversations shifted behavior by shifting moral beliefs.

We found that 43% (95% CI [33%, 58%]) of the immediate treatment effect on the dietary choice was mediated by change in the meat belief (indirect effect: a × b = 0.080, 95% CI [0.063, 0.098], p < .001; direct effect: c ′ = 0.105, 95% CI [0.064, 0.147], p < .001).

text.text: Similarly, 37% (95% CI [21%, 79%]) of the immediate treatment effect on donations to the AMF was mediated by change in the charity belief (a × b = 0.61 cents, 95% CI [0.42, 0.81], p < .001; c ′ = 1.06 cents, 95% CI [0.15, 1.91], p = .030).

text.text: We also found that 83% (95% CI [48%, 237%]) of the follow-up treatment effect on the dietary choice was mediated by immediate change in agreement (a × b = 0.064, 95% CI [0.046, 0.085], p < .001; c ′ = 0.013, 95% CI [-0.037, 0.061], p = .648), and 28% (95% CI [13%, 71%]) was mediated by follow-up change in agreement (a × b = 0.022, 95% CI [0.012, 0.034], p < .001; c ′ = 0.055, 95% CI [0.009, 0.100], p = .024; in a separate mediation model with follow-up belief change as the mediator).

text.text: While there was no significant total effect on donations to the AMF at one-month follow-up, moral belief immediately post-treatment significantly mediated the effect (indirect effect: a × b = 0.65, 95% CI [0.42, 0.91], p < .001), but with an opposite non-significant direct effect (c ′ = -0.66, 95% CI [-1.58, 0.29], p = .202), with the same general result with follow-up moral beliefs as the mediator (indirect effect: a × b = 0.21, 95% CI [0.03, 0.40], p = .010, direct effect: c ′ = -0.21, 95% CI [-1.12, 0.66], p = .686).

text.text: Immediate post-conversation ratings of AI understanding, respectfulness, and novelty of AI arguments were generally weak mediators of the effects on beliefs and behavior (SI S1.2.5).

We also examined univariate linear treatment effect moderation on a set of pre-treatment variables: demographics (age, gender, education, income, and race), cognitive style (openmindedness to evidence and cognitive reflection), political orientation (ideology and party identification), AI trust, and all pre-treatment moral beliefs.

After Holm correction for multiple comparisons, the treatment effect on immediate change in the meat belief was positively moderated by AI trust (b = 2.16 points per Likert scale point, Holm-adjusted p < .001) and negatively moderated by the pre-treatment meat belief (b = -0.09 points per 0-100 pre-treatment belief point, Holm-adjusted p = .050).

text.text: No other moderator of the immediate prosocial effects was significant, and no moderator was significant at one-month follow-up (SI S1.2.3 and Table S8).

text.text: Pilot results.
Figures 2 and 3 also report the results from a pilot study (N = 500) that used each condition as an active control for the other rather than including a pure control.
text.formatted: Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> also report the results from a pilot study (N = 500) that used each condition as an active control for the other rather than including a pure control.

text.text: This pilot study also found significant immediate effects on beliefs (the charity belief: d = 0.36, p < .001; the meat belief: d = 0.47, p < .001; SI S2.2.1 and Figure S10) and behaviors (dietary choice: 25.04pp, p < .001; donation: d = 0.20, p = .024; SI S2.2.2 and Figure S11), but presented mixed results in relation to persistence: belief change was not significant at one-month follow-up (meat: p = .598; charity: p = .055), nor were donations to the AMF (p = .615), although the dietary choice was (10.66pp, p = .014).
text.formatted: This pilot study also found significant immediate effects on beliefs (the charity belief: d = 0.36, p < .001; the meat belief: d = 0.47, p < .001; SI S2.2.1 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S10</ref>) and behaviors (dietary choice: 25.04pp, p < .001; donation: d = 0.20, p = .024; SI S2.2.2 and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S11</ref>), but presented mixed results in relation to persistence: belief change was not significant at one-month follow-up (meat: p = .598; charity: p = .055), nor were donations to the AMF (p = .615), although the dietary choice was (10.66pp, p = .014).

text.text: Here we show that the estimates from this pilot study in each analogous treatment condition were similar (or larger) in magnitude to the present study, but comparisons between the two conditions were not significant at follow-up largely due to reduced power, as well as the absence of a pure control condition which may have resulted in spillover between the two conditions.
The design of the present study addresses both these issues, showing clear evidence of persistent effects on prosocial moral beliefs and behavior one month later.

We also note that these two studies used different prompts and AI models (pilot: GPT-4o; main: Grok 4.5; SI S2.1.2 and S1.1.1), demonstrating the generalizability of the prosocial persuasion results across AI models and prompts.
We include a complete write-up of the methods and results of the pilot study in SI S2.
Conversations with the AI also produced significant shifts in moral beliefs and behaviors in the antisocial conditions (Figures 4 and 5).
text.formatted: Conversations with the AI also produced significant shifts in moral beliefs and behaviors in the antisocial conditions (Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref> and <ref type="figure">5</ref>).

text.text: We first look at the effects of the AI conversation that argued that 'In the US today, using violence to advance political goals is not morally wrong' (political violence conversation condition).

For ethical reasons, our 'behavioral' measure of political violence stopped short of any actual behavior, with participants instead rating their attitudes and intentions in relation to a hypothetical vignette designed to be realistic in the current US political climate.

Participants read a fictional news report in which, during a contested recount after the 2028 presidential election, a crowd of supporters of the participant's own party forced its way into a Michigan election center to stop the count, injuring four police officers and an election worker (for the full vignette, see SI S1.1.3).
They then rated, as the primary preregistered outcome, whether, if they were there, they would personally force their way into the election center with the crowd (0-100).
As secondary outcomes, they also rated their support for and justification of the crowd's actions and whether those responsible should face criminal charges.
We found immediate effects on moral belief and on the vignette outcomes.

The political violence conversation significantly reduced agreement that in the US today using violence to advance political goals is morally wrong compared to the control (d = 1.05, p < .001; Figure 4A), and significantly increased willingness to join the violent crowd (d = 0.23, p = .014; Figure 4B).
text.formatted: The political violence conversation significantly reduced agreement that in the US today using violence to advance political goals is morally wrong compared to the control (d = 1.05, p < .001; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4A</ref>), and significantly increased willingness to join the violent crowd (d = 0.23, p = .014; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4B</ref>).

text.text: The political violence conversation also significantly increased support (d = 0.32, p < .001) and justification (d = 0.21, p = .010) of the violence in the vignette relative to the control, and reduced participants' likelihood of saying that the perpetrators should face criminal charges (unadjusted means 80% vs. 87%; p = .019).

text.text: A preregistered composite of the support, justification, and punishment judgments was also higher in the political-violence condition than control (d = 0.29, p = .001).
Belief change mediated 71% of the effect on willingness to join the crowd (a × b = 3.32, 95% CI [1.91, 4.99], c ′ = 1.32, 95% CI [-2.04, 4.59], p = .462; SI S1.2.4).
There was no treatment effect moderation significant after Holm correction (SI S1.2.3 and Table S8).

text.text: Lying.

We now turn to the effects of the AI conversation that argued that 'Deceiving others for your own financial gain is not morally wrong' (lying conversation condition) on the lying belief and the coin-flip task.
The lying conversation significantly reduced agreement that deceiving others for one's own financial gain is morally wrong compared to the control (d = 0.68, p < .001; Figure 5A).
text.formatted: The lying conversation significantly reduced agreement that deceiving others for one's own financial gain is morally wrong compared to the control (d = 0.68, p < .001; Figure <ref type="figure">5A</ref>).

text.text: As a behavioral measure of deceiving others for one's own gain, participants flipped a virtual coin that was rigged to always first land on tails (and fair thereafter) and were paid a bonus if they reported that it landed heads.

Surprisingly, the lying conversation significantly decreased reporting of heads in the coin task by 4.3 percentage points relative to the control (unadjusted means 7% vs. 11%; p = .012; Figure 5B); that is, the lying conversation made participants less likely to lie to benefit themselves.
text.formatted: Surprisingly, the lying conversation significantly decreased reporting of heads in the coin task by 4.3 percentage points relative to the control (unadjusted means 7% vs. 11%; p = .012; Figure <ref type="figure">5B</ref>); that is, the lying conversation made participants less likely to lie to benefit themselves.

text.text: To explore why behavior in the coin-flip shifted against the intended direction of persuasion-and in the opposite direction of the average moral belief change-we examined post-hoc the relationship between the behavioral measures and pre-treatment belief in the control condition, where none of the behavioral measures were targeted by persuasion.

We found significant relationships in the expected directions for all domains (meat: r = .46, p < .001; charity: r = .17, p < .001; political violence: r = -.29, p < .001) except for lying (r = -.02, p = .61).
text.formatted: We found significant relationships in the expected directions for all domains (meat: r = .46, p < .001; charity: r = .17, p < .001; political violence: r = -.29, p < .001) except for lying (r = -.02, p = .61).

text.text: Similarly, the treatment effect on the coin-flip task was not mediated by belief change (indirect effect: ab = 0.005, 95% CI [-0.005, 0.015], p = .31; direct effect: c ′ = -0.049, 95% CI [-0.085, -0.013], p = .008), whereas belief change carried a significant share of the behavioral effect in every other domain (meat 43%, charity 37%, political violence 71%; SI Table S9).
text.formatted: Similarly, the treatment effect on the coin-flip task was not mediated by belief change (indirect effect: ab = 0.005, 95% CI [-0.005, 0.015], p = .31; direct effect: c ′ = -0.049, 95% CI [-0.085, -0.013], p = .008), whereas belief change carried a significant share of the behavioral effect in every other domain (meat 43%, charity 37%, political violence 71%; SI Table <ref type="table">S9</ref>).

text.text: Together, these results suggest that our measure of the broad belief that 'Deceiving others for your own financial gain is morally wrong' did not capture whatever guided behavior in the coin-flip task.
This may explain why belief and behavior diverged, but not why behavior moved in the opposite direction.

The text from the human-AI conversations suggests a possible explanation for this: the broad belief measured may encompass forms of deception that differ from the direct lie required by the coin-flip task, allowing the AI to weaken the former while reinforcing moral opposition to the latter.

Indeed, in many cases the AI agent pursued its goal of arguing that deceiving others for financial gain was not morally wrong by defending a softer class of deception-omissions and exaggerations during negotiations or sales-rather than the more direct falsehood measured by the coin-flip task (directly stating a falsehood that enriches you at another's expense).

In doing so, the AI often either did not discuss direct lies at all, or cited direct lies as different from the conduct it was defending, explicitly or implicitly treating such direct lies as morally wrong and so reinforcing the belief most relevant to the coin-flip task.
Indeed, in post-hoc analyses using three independent LLM coders (majority agreement; see SI S1.1.6), we find that 32.8% of conversations did not mention these direct lies at all.

Of the conversations that did, 42.4% argued that such a direct lie was separate and different from the softer class of deception, reinforcing direct lies as morally wrong, whereas 57.2% of the time the model argued that direct lies were also not morally wrong.
Most notably, when it defended the direct lie as morally acceptable, participants reported heads at 10.6%, similar to the other conditions.
When it reinforced that the direct lies were wrong, participants reported heads at 3.6%, much lower than all other conditions.
These analyses, however, may suffer from endogeneity issues, and are offered for exploratory and hypothesis-generating purposes to understand the unexpected direction of the coin-flip effect.

Finally, moderation analyses found just one significant moderator after Holm correction: participants who answered the cognitive reflection item correctly showed a smaller treatment effect on change in the lying belief (b = 7.66 points, Holm-adjusted p = .021; SI S1.2.3 and Table S8).

We classified these reasons for potentially persuadable participants-i.e., those who initially rejected the position the AI argued for (Figure 6).

text.text: Among participants initially skeptical that eating meat is wrong (n = 703), the most common justifications were that eating meat is natural (33.3%) or necessary for health (33.3%), followed by the view that it is acceptable if the meat is ethically sourced (conditional; 26.0%) and that it is not a moral issue (amoral; 17.1%).

Among those initially skeptical that not giving to charity is wrong (n = 612), financial constraints dominated (60.0%), followed by the view that giving is good but not required (supererogatory; 20.6%) and skepticism that charity works (15.2%).

Among participants who initially agreed that deceiving others for financial gain is wrong (n = 376), the most common reasons were that it harms others (37.5%), that deception is wrong as an absolute rule (22.9%), and that the gain is unearned (22.6%).

Among those who initially agreed that political violence is wrong (n = 191), the most common reasons were that violence is always wrong (31.9%), that other non-violent methods of change are available (27.2%), that violence does not work (24.1%), and that it harms people (24.1%).

Because these reasons were written before the conversation, we can also ask (post-hoc) whether people who gave a particular reason changed their belief more or less in response to the AI conversation (SI S1.2.11 and Figure S9).

text.text: In every domain, participants moved in the direction of persuasion whichever reason they gave, and most differences between reasons were small.

The exception was charity: participants who doubted that charity works (skepticism) or who held that the problem needs structural change rather than individual giving (systemic) changed less than those who did not give these reasons.

text.text: We also examined, descriptively, how the AI agent argued, by rating the extent to which it used each of five persuasive strategies in every treatment conversation (Methods; SI S1.1.5; Figure 7).
text.formatted: We also examined, descriptively, how the AI agent argued, by rating the extent to which it used each of five persuasive strategies in every treatment conversation (Methods; SI S1.1.5; Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref>).

text.text: In all four domains, the AI relied heavily on moral principles and on analogies and re-framing.
The domains differed, however, in the AI's use of the other persuasive strategies.

Meat conversations drew most on evidence and facts, consistent with the many factual claims that bear on this question (for example, about meat consumption and health, animal neurology, and farming practices).

Emotional appeals were more central in the prosocial conversations but less so in the antisocial ones, although there was substantial variation between conversations of the same condition, particularly for the antisocial conversations.
Logical-consistency arguments, which point out conflicts within the participant's own commitments and beliefs, were most common in the political-violence and meat conversations.
Our results show that the persuasive capacity of human-AI dialogues extends to the moral domain, shifting not just beliefs about what is, but about what ought to be.
Brief conversations with a persuasive AI agent shifted moral beliefs and related incentive-compatible behavior and behavioral intentions across all four domains we tested.

While previous work has shown that LLMs can change factual beliefs, such as conspiracy and climate change beliefs (Costello et al., 2024; Hornsey et al., 2025), and even political attitudes (Hackenburg et al., 2025; H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025), we are among the first to show these effects in purely moral domains, particularly for general moral beliefs that guide everyday behavior (but see Landes et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026; Teng et al., 2026, which show AI moral persuasion on moral judgments, not behavior, in relation to specific hypothetical scenarios).

Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025)</ref>, we are among the first to show these effects in purely moral domains, particularly for general moral beliefs that guide everyday behavior (but see <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Landes et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lyu et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Teng et al., 2026, which</ref> show AI moral persuasion on moral judgments, not behavior, in relation to specific hypothetical scenarios).

text.text: Indeed, we demonstrate that persuasion targeting just these generalized moral beliefs can change related behaviors.
This result contrasts with recent work showing that AI persuasion targeted towards changing particular behaviors does not necessarily result in concomitant attitude change (Hackenburg et al., 2026).

Together these findings show how behavior change can be affected via multiple pathways: directly (e.g., via specific asks for behavior; Hackenburg et al., 2026) or indirectly through targeting underlying moral beliefs.

text.text: Our results also complement prior work showing that extensive philosophy instruction in educational settings can alter moral beliefs (Oktar et al., 2023) and behaviors (Schwitzgebel et al., 2023), demonstrating that such change can also be achieved through short human-AI dialogues.
text.formatted: Our results also complement prior work showing that extensive philosophy instruction in educational settings can alter moral beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Oktar et al., 2023)</ref> and behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schwitzgebel et al., 2023)</ref>, demonstrating that such change can also be achieved through short human-AI dialogues.

text.text: Further, we show that these effects were not merely transient.
One month later, treatment effects remained significant for the meat belief, the charity belief, and the dietary choice, retaining roughly a third of the immediate effects.

These results suggest that while moral beliefs are often considered deeply held and resistant to change (Stanley et al., 2018), human-AI dialogues can shift them, and that these shifts can have lasting consequences, even on incentive-compatible behaviors.
text.formatted: These results suggest that while moral beliefs are often considered deeply held and resistant to change <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Stanley et al., 2018)</ref>, human-AI dialogues can shift them, and that these shifts can have lasting consequences, even on incentive-compatible behaviors.

text.text: Effect persistence was, however, not universal: the effect on donations did not survive to follow-up, raising questions about which beliefs and behaviors may be most susceptible to durable change from AI persuasion.
Further investigating which beliefs and behaviors are more or less responsive to these effects is a fruitful direction for future work.
Our results also show that the moral persuasiveness of human-AI dialogues can be harnessed for both prosocial and harmful ends.

Conversations arguing that deceiving others for financial gain and that political violence are not morally wrong produced large reductions in belief that these acts are morally wrong (d = 0.68 and d = 1.05)-significantly larger, on average, than the belief effects observed in the prosocial conditions (on the original 0-100 belief scale, post-hoc, SI S1.2.7).

One speculative explanation for this asymmetry is that prosocial moral persuasion may tend to be prescriptive (creating a new positive obligation of what one should do), whereas antisocial persuasion may tend to relax a proscriptive rule (removing a prohibition on what one should not do) (Janoff-Bulman et al., 2009).
text.formatted: One speculative explanation for this asymmetry is that prosocial moral persuasion may tend to be prescriptive (creating a new positive obligation of what one should do), whereas antisocial persuasion may tend to relax a proscriptive rule (removing a prohibition on what one should not do) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Janoff-Bulman et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Another is that persuasion may be subject to motivated moral reasoning that favors people's self-interest Uhlmann et al., 2009.
text.formatted: Another is that persuasion may be subject to motivated moral reasoning that favors people's self-interest <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Uhlmann et al., 2009</ref>.

text.text: Future research should explore whether such an asymmetry in the effectiveness of prosocial and harmful AI moral persuasion exists more generally.
Regardless, our results give no reason to expect that moral convictions against harmful acts are especially protected from AI persuasion.
These results bear directly on AI safety.
First, the AI model (Grok 4.5) used in the present study is publicly available and widely used.

That it was both willing and able to persuade people that political violence in the US today and lying for financial gain are not morally wrong raises questions about the robustness and effectiveness of current model safeguards against harmful AI persuasion, and suggests that the capability to deploy such AI agents at scale is already a reality.

Second, our results show that the downstream behavioral effects of AI conversation intervention are not always predictable, as evidenced by the fact that the lying conversation reduced beliefs that deceiving others for financial gain is morally wrong, but reduced falsely reporting heads in the lie-incentivized coin-flip task.
This unpredictability is itself a safety concern.

If the effects of AI persuasion cannot be reliably predicted, then neither the stated aims of its prompt, nor its effects on any single measured outcome are guaranteed to inform its actual consequences.
One practical implication is that safety evaluations cannot infer behavioral risk from belief change alone, and even relying on single behavioral outcomes may be limited.
Indeed, thorough safety evaluations should measure behavior across several outcomes and domains, particularly those where the moral belief and related actions are closely linked.
In addition, our results raise hypotheses about the mechanisms of moral persuasion that should be the subject of future investigation.

Our results suggest that factual correction may be one major mechanism leading to moral belief change: our text analysis revealed that the meat conversations relied more heavily on evidence and factual information than charity conversations (Figure 7), and we generally saw larger and more persistent effects on meat beliefs and behaviors than for charity beliefs and behaviors.
text.formatted: Our results suggest that factual correction may be one major mechanism leading to moral belief change: our text analysis revealed that the meat conversations relied more heavily on evidence and factual information than charity conversations (Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref>), and we generally saw larger and more persistent effects on meat beliefs and behaviors than for charity beliefs and behaviors.

text.text: Further, the most common justifications participants offered for eating meat-appeals to naturalness and biological necessity (Figure 6A)-are precisely the kinds of beliefs amenable to factual correction.
text.formatted: Further, the most common justifications participants offered for eating meat-appeals to naturalness and biological necessity (Figure <ref type="figure">6A</ref>)-are precisely the kinds of beliefs amenable to factual correction.

text.text: The charity domain, by contrast, may be more resistant to this mechanism, as the dominant justifications given by participants against a positive charitable obligation reflect more purely evaluative disagreements (e.g., that charitable giving is 'good' but not obligatory), or situational factors (e.g., financial constraints) that are less susceptible to factual updating.
This suggests a mechanistic account where moral persuasion may be more effective when it is embedded in factual disagreements that can be corrected, than when the persuasion is purely evaluative.

Such an account would accord with research showing that facts, reason and evidence are the major persuasive mechanism at play for factual and attitudinal domains (Costello et al., 2025; H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025), and even for charity-related behaviors (White et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such an account would accord with research showing that facts, reason and evidence are the major persuasive mechanism at play for factual and attitudinal domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Costello et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">H. Lin, Czarnek, et al., 2025)</ref>, and even for charity-related behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(White et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, the fact that persuasion ocurred broadly, and that there was variation in strategy use both between and within domains, suggests that the best strategy for moral persuasion may indeed be very domain and person dependent.
Future work experimentally varying both persuasive strategy and moral domain will be needed to test these mechanistic hypotheses directly.
Finally, we note some interpretive limitations of the belief and behavioral measures used in this study.
Changes in the belief items could reflect demand, consistency, acquiescence, or salience effects rather than genuine belief change.
However, comparisons against the control condition and the general stability of nontarget moral beliefs rule out effects of AI interaction, general moral discussion, or repeated measurement.

Prior work also suggests that demand effects are small or absent in online studies (de Quidt et al., 2018; Mummolo & Peterson, 2019), including studies of moral judgment (Woodley et al., 2026), and that demand, acquiescence, and salience effects are minimal even in similarly strong AI-conversation interventions (Costello et al., 2025), suggesting such explanations are very unlikely to explain the medium-to-large effects observed in this study.
text.formatted: Prior work also suggests that demand effects are small or absent in online studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(de Quidt et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Mummolo & Peterson, 2019)</ref>, including studies of moral judgment <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Woodley et al., 2026)</ref>, and that demand, acquiescence, and salience effects are minimal even in similarly strong AI-conversation interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Costello et al., 2025)</ref>, suggesting such explanations are very unlikely to explain the medium-to-large effects observed in this study.

text.text: The behavioral measures raise a similar possibility.
Significant behavioral effects of the AI conversation are consistent with belief change as a pathway to behavior, but these measures nonetheless remain open to other readings.
Selecting the plant-based voucher, for example, could reflect curiosity or a temporary interest prompted by the meat conversation rather than value change about the morality of eating meat.

Yet, the persistence of these effects, their mediation by belief change, and the fact that the models were instructed to discuss general moral beliefs with no reference to the measured behaviors, nonetheless are suggestive evidence of genuine moral belief change affecting behavior.
Overall, we show the power of AI persuasion to meaningfully shift moral beliefs and related behaviors toward both prosocial and harmful ends, with the prosocial effects persisting one month later.
As conversational AI continues to become embedded in everyday life, questions about whether and in which directions these systems should exert moral influence, and who decides, will become pressing.
Governing AI's capacity to shape human values will be essential.
3438 participants from the United States were recruited through Cloud Research.

Of these, 281 withdrew prior to randomization, 66 failed a preregistered pre-treatment attention check, and 6 failed a bot check, leaving an intention-to-treat (ITT) sample of 3085.113 withdrew after randomization, leaving a final sample of 2972 (1494 women, 1468 men, 6 other, 4 NA; M age = 41.47, SD = 13.88, range: 18-84 years).

We invited all timepoint 1 completers in the charity, meat, and control conditions (N = 2381) to participate in a follow-up study approximately 1-month later. 1926 of these participants (80.9%; 983 women, 934 men, 5 other, 4 NA; M age = 42.64, SD = 14.11, range: 18-83 years) returned to follow-up on average 29.7 days (SD = 2.77) after their initial session (22.9-40.5 days; initial study: 2-12 September 2026, follow-up: 5-14 October 2026).
Of these, 1924 completed both follow-up behavioral measures and form the follow-up analysis sample.
All participants gave informed consent to participate (see Ethics, below).

Participants were paid $3.00 at timepoint 1 and $0.60 at timepoint 2, plus additional bonuses at each timepoint that depended on their responses to the charity donation (up to 20 cents), the dietary choice (one participant randomly selected to receive the beef or plant-based burger voucher corresponding to their choice), and the lie-incentivized coin-flip task (20 cents).

We did observe some general predictors of attrition: education predicted completion of the initial survey (Holm-adjusted p = .013), and age (Holm-adjusted p < .001), income (Holmadjusted p = .026), and identifying as White (Holm-adjusted p = .045) predicted return at follow-up (SI Table S5).

Demographics and pre-treatment covariates.
Participants completed the study online via Cloud Research.
The experiment was run on Qualtrics using vegapunk (H. Lin, Costello, & Safo, 2025) to facilitate the human-AI conversations.

text.text: After providing informed consent, participants responded to demographic questions covering age, gender, race, education level, income, and political orientation and identity.

Pre-treatment covariate measures were also collected, including trust in AI, the bat & ball question from the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT; Frederick, 2005), and two items from the Actively Open-Minded Thinking about Evidence scale (AOT-E; Pennycook et al., 2020) (SI S1.1.2).
