text.text: The experimental flow is summarized in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The experimental flow is summarized in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Participants first rated their initial beliefs about five target claims (SI Table S1)-four moral and one non-moral control-on a scale from 0-100, as pre-treatment baseline measurements.
text.formatted: Participants first rated their initial beliefs about five target claims (SI Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>)-four moral and one non-moral control-on a scale from 0-100, as pre-treatment baseline measurements.

text.text: Participants were then randomized into four treatment conditions and one control condition, each corresponding to one target claim.
They were first asked to "give one or more reasons for your response" to their target claim in free text.

In each treatment condition, participants then had a 5-round conversation with an AI agent (Grok 4.5) that was prompted with their rating and reasons and instructed to persuade them in relation to their target claim.

In the control condition, participants had a persuasive conversation with the same AI agent about the non-moral control claim (their preference for summer or winter), in which the AI agent was prompted to persuade them against their initial reported preference.
For full prompts, see SI S1.1.1.

The conversation was introduced to participants as a dialogue with an advanced AI about topics they had already answered questions about, to understand 'how humans and AI can engage around complicated topics' (SI S1.1.1).

Following the 5-round conversation, participants completed all outcome measures (below), followed by three ratings of the conversation (how well the AI understood their perspective, how respectful it was, and whether it made points they had not thought of before; SI S1.1.2).

Participants in the two antisocial conditions (political violence and lying) were then immediately debriefed: they were told that the AI had been "given a hidden instruction ... to persuade you that [target] is NOT morally wrong".

They then had a "corrective" conversation with another AI agent, where they were told that "the AI has been given the transcript of your earlier conversation, and it has been asked to point out where that earlier conversation may have been one-sided or misleading, and to argue that [target] IS morally wrong."
Participants in these conditions then re-rated their focal moral belief (SI S1.2.10).
All participants then gave free-text feedback about the experiment before completion.
One-month follow-up.
All completers in the control, meat, and charity conditions were invited to complete a follow-up survey approximately one month later.
Here, participants re-completed the meat and charity moral beliefs and behaviors.

In addition, they completed a preregistered secondary outcome measure for each condition: the self-reported number of times they ate meat in the last month, and the self-reported dollar amount they gave to charity in the last month (SI S1.2.9).
Participants first completed the moral belief measures, then the behavior measures, and then the self-reported behavior measures before finishing the experiment.
Within each block, the order of the meat and charity items was counterbalanced across participants.
Completers in the lying and political-violence conditions were recontacted separately to check for any persisting change after the corrective procedure (SI S1.2.10).
Each treatment condition had two associated primary outcome variables: a moral belief and a downstream behavior.
Participants completed all outcome measures regardless of their condition.
For the moral belief outcomes, participants rated their agreement with the target claim exactly as they did pre-treatment.
We use "moral belief" for agreement with these general claims (for example, that eating meat is morally wrong), reserving the term "moral judgment" for evaluations of specific cases.
The behavioral outcomes were designed to be, where possible, incentive-compatible choices related to each moral claim: • Dietary choice (meat).
Participants chose whether they would prefer a voucher for a beef burger or a plant-based burger, with one participant randomly selected to receive the voucher they chose.
The order of the two options was counterbalanced.
• Charitable donation (charity).
Participants received a 20-cent bonus and chose how much of it (0-20 cents) to donate to the Against Malaria Foundation, keeping the rest.
• Coin flip (lying).
Participants flipped a virtual coin embedded in the survey, with a 20-cent bonus for reporting heads.

The coin was rigged so that the first flip always landed on tails (later flips were random), so reporting heads was a dishonest report (for a similar coin-flip dishonesty task, see Rand & Yoeli, 2024).
text.formatted: The coin was rigged so that the first flip always landed on tails (later flips were random), so reporting heads was a dishonest report (for a similar coin-flip dishonesty task, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Rand & Yoeli, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: All participants were paid the 20-cent bonus at the end of the study regardless of their report.
• Political-violence participation (political violence).

Participants read a realistic but hypothetical news report in which a crowd of supporters of their own party forced its way into a Michigan election center during a contested recount after the 2028 presidential election, injuring police officers and an election worker.
They then rated whether they would personally force their way into the election center with the crowd (0 = definitely would not,100 = definitely would).
This is a self-reported intention rather than an incentivized choice.
Participants also rated their support for and justification of the crowd's actions, and whether the people arrested should face criminal charges (preregistered secondary outcomes).
As preregistered, we also analyzed a composite of these three items, the mean of their z-scores, with the criminal-charges item reverse-coded so that higher scores are more favorable to the violence.
The full vignette and items are in SI S1.1.3.
Participants first completed the moral belief measures, then the behavior measures.

Within each block, the order of the questions was counterbalanced among the meat, charity, and lying conditions (all 6 permutations were equally likely), with the political violence item always appearing last.
This ordering was consistent across the blocks, at both pre-and post-treatment.

Primary inference focused on estimating the causal impact (the average treatment effect, ATE) of the persuasive AI conversation on change in the target moral belief and on the target behavior relative to the control condition.

We conducted OLS regressions, with HC2 robust standard errors, regressing each outcome on condition (treatment-coded) as the key independent variable and controlling for centered pre-treatment belief, including its interaction with condition (i.e., the Lin estimator (W. Lin, 2013)), and a dummy variable for their counterbalanced question order.
These analyses were repeated on one-month follow-up outcomes, including the secondary self-reported behavior measures (SI S1.2.9).
As preregistered, we did not correct for multiple comparisons among these primary analyses, as each is a different pre-specified estimand of interest.

These models also estimate the ATE for every treatment-control comparison on each measure, allowing us to examine "spillover" effects of each treatment on non-target moral beliefs and behaviors (e.g., the effect of the lying conversation on meat beliefs and behaviors).
We preregistered these as exploratory analyses and test them with Holm-adjusted p-values, applied across the 12 spillover contrasts separately for beliefs and for behaviors (SI S1.2.8 and Figure S8).
text.formatted: We preregistered these as exploratory analyses and test them with Holm-adjusted p-values, applied across the 12 spillover contrasts separately for beliefs and for behaviors (SI S1.2.8 and Figure <ref type="figure">S8</ref>).

text.text: In addition, we ran preregistered exploratory mediation analyses of behavior by moral belief and treatment effect moderation analyses (SI S1.2.4 and S1.2.3).
All models used HC2 robust standard errors, with two-sided hypothesis tests with α = 0.05.

We report standardized effect sizes as Cohen's d, with the model estimated ATE divided by pooled pre-treatment standard deviation when available (i.e., for beliefs) or the control group standard deviation immediately post treatment when not (i.e., for behaviors).

text.text: To characterize the persuasive approaches used by the AI across the multi-round conversations, we rated each treatment conversation on five strategies: Evidence & Facts (descriptive claims about how the world is, such as statistics, research findings, and consequences), Logical Consistency (arguing that rejecting the claim conflicts with a belief or value the participant already holds), Moral Principles (invoking a general moral standard from which the claim follows), Emotional Appeal (evoking feelings such as sympathy, guilt, or pride), and Analogies & Reframing (asking the participant to see the issue through a different case, perspective, or description).
text.formatted: To characterize the persuasive approaches used by the AI across the multi-round conversations, we rated each treatment conversation on five strategies: Evidence & Facts (descriptive claims about how the world is, such as statistics, research findings, and consequences), Logical Consistency (arguing that rejecting the claim conflicts with a belief or value the participant already holds), Moral Principles (invoking a general moral standard from which the claim follows), Emotional Appeal (evoking feelings such as sympathy, guilt, or pride), and Analogies & Reframing (asking the participant to see the issue through a different case, perspective, or description).

text.text: Each full conversation (the participant's initial reasons and all AI and participant messages, with only the AI's messages assessed) was independently rated by three LLMs: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), GPT-5.5 (OpenAI), and Grok 4.7 (xAI), each with high reasoning effort.
Each strategy was rated on a four-point ordinal scale reflecting the extent of use: none (0), low (1), moderate (2), and high (3).
The strategy score for each conversation is the mean rating across the three models, reported in Figure 7.
text.formatted: The strategy score for each conversation is the mean rating across the three models, reported in Figure <ref type="figure">7</ref>.

text.text: The three models were at most one scale point apart on 94.5-99.8% of conversations, depending on the strategy, with mean ICC(2,k) = .66 (range .18 for moral principles, where ratings had little variance, to .87 for logical consistency; SI Table S4).
text.formatted: The three models were at most one scale point apart on 94.5-99.8% of conversations, depending on the strategy, with mean ICC(2,k) = .66 (range .18 for moral principles, where ratings had little variance, to .87 for logical consistency; SI Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: The codebook and prompts are in SI S1.1.5.
Before the AI conversation, participants wrote a free-text justification for their focal moral belief.
Three LLMs independently classified each response at temperature 0, using structured JSON output: Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic), GPT-4.1 (OpenAI), and DeepSeek V3.2 (DeepSeek).
Categories were multi-label, and a category was coded as present if at least two of the three models marked it present.

We report these analyses only for participants who initially disagreed with the position the AI argued for (pre-treatment score ≤ 50 in the prosocial conditions and ≥ 50 in the antisocial conditions).
Agreement was high: the three models gave the same judgment on a given category for 86.4-99.7% of texts (SI Table S3).
text.formatted: Agreement was high: the three models gave the same judgment on a given category for 86.4-99.7% of texts (SI Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: See SI S1.1.4.
The study was approved as exempt by the MIT Committee on the Use of Human Subjects in Research (#E-7980).
Because the AI argued for antisocial moral positions, the study included several safeguards.
The consent form warned participants that the study might challenge their beliefs and that information presented to them might be one-sided or inaccurate, and would be explained at the end.

In the lying and political-violence conditions, the AI argued only for the abstract moral claim and was instructed not to advocate, encourage, or help plan any particular act of deception or violence, or to describe means or methods of violence (SI Table S1).
text.formatted: In the lying and political-violence conditions, the AI argued only for the abstract moral claim and was instructed not to advocate, encourage, or help plan any particular act of deception or violence, or to describe means or methods of violence (SI Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: The political-violence behavioral measure was a hypothetical vignette, and the coin-flip bonus was paid to everyone regardless of their report.
In addition, participants in the antisocial conditions were immediately debriefed that the AI was instructed to persuade them in a particular direction and may have thus been onesided and misleading.
They then had a "corrective conversation" which reversed most of the average belief shift before they left the original study.

They were also recontacted one month later to assess whether any harmful belief or attitude change from baseline was present, and engaged in a further corrective conversation if necessary (i.e., if they did not give the maximum rating of 100/100 at follow-up).

The corrective procedure was largely effective: beliefs that the target acts were morally wrong remained high, almost all participants were not reliably below their pretreatment belief beyond measurement error, and vignette intentions and attitudes in the political-violence arm were no higher than in the control arm, even though the general political-violence moral belief remained about 5 points below baseline.
For details and analysis of the corrective conversations and follow-up in the antisocial treatment arms see SI S1.2.10.
Finally, fewer participants were assigned to these conditions than to the prosocial conditions (lying 393, political violence 198, compared to ∼800 in the meat, charity, and control conditions).
Figure 1.

Study design.All participants rated four moral claims and a season preference, then were randomly assigned to a five-round conversation with Grok 4.5 (N = 2,972), which was given their stated reasons for their initial rating.
Prosocial conversations argued that eating meat (n = 791) or not giving to charity (n = 795) is morally wrong.
Antisocial conversations argued that deceiving others for financial gain (n = 393) or using violence to advance political goals (n = 198) is not morally wrong.
The control conversation (n = 795) argued for the participant's non-preferred season.

Immediately afterward, all participants rerated the moral claims and then completed four behavioral measures in counterbalanced order: a choice between beef and plant-based burger vouchers, a donation to the Against Malaria Foundation, an incentivized coin-flip honesty task, and willingness to join the crowd in a political-violence vignette.
Control and prosocial participants repeated the meat and charity belief and behavior measures at a one-month follow-up (n = 1,926).

Antisocial participants were instead debriefed immediately, had a corrective AI conversation that flagged misleading arguments and argued that lying or political violence is morally wrong, and re-rated their target belief.
As an ethical safeguard, they were recontacted about one month later to check for any persisting belief or attitude change.
Those rating their target belief below 100 had a further corrective conversation, then re-rated the target belief and, in the political-violence condition, the vignette items.
